title: 11. Observability & SRE: Health Checks
summary: Health checks are automated, periodic probes that ask a service "are you able to serve traffic?" so that orchestrators and load balancers can route around failing instances without human intervention — the single most…
objectives: What is the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe, and why must they be separate?
Should a readiness probe check downstream dependencies? What are the trade-offs?
What happens if you set the liveness probe interval too short (e.g., 1 second)?
Explain graceful shutdown and why it is essential for zero-downtime deploys.

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Health checks are automated, periodic probes that ask a service "are you able to serve traffic?" so that orchestrators and load balancers can route around failing instances without human intervention — the single most important mechanism for achieving self-healing in distributed systems.
A health check is an HTTP endpoint (or gRPC method, or TCP probe) that the service exposes, which an external prober (Kubernetes kubelet, AWS ELB, Envoy, HAProxy) calls on a fixed interval — typically every 5–10 seconds — to decide whether the service is healthy enough to receive traffic. The probe returns a status code (200 OK, 503 Service Unavailable) and optionally a JSON body describing the state of internal dependencies. The prober uses the response to make routing decisions: a healthy instance stays in the load-balancer pool; an unhealthy instance is removed until it recovers. The mechanism is conceptually simple but operationally subtle, because the question "are you healthy?" has at least two distinct meanings that must be probed separately, and conflating them causes cascading failures.

The foundational distinction is liveness versus readiness. A liveness probe asks "is this process alive and able to make progress, or is it deadlocked and should be restarted?" A readiness probe asks "is this process ready to serve traffic right now, or should the load balancer stop sending requests until it recovers?" The two answers can differ: a service that is alive (the process is running, the event loop is turning over) but not ready (its database connection pool is empty because the database is briefly unreachable) should not be restarted — restarting would not help, because the new instance would face the same empty pool — but it should be removed from the load balancer so requests do not pile up against it. Conversely, a service that is deadlocked (the process is running but the event loop is stuck) should be restarted, because restarting is the only way to recover. Kubernetes formalizes this with two probe types: `livenessProbe` triggers a pod restart on failure; `readinessProbe` removes the pod from the service's endpoint list on failure but does not restart it. The mistake teams make is to use one probe for both purposes, which produces either unnecessary restarts (liveness probe that fails when a dependency is briefly unreachable) or stuck traffic (readiness probe that should have triggered a restart but only de-routed).

The second concept is shallow versus deep checks. A shallow check answers "is the process running and the endpoint reachable?" with minimal work — typically returning 200 OK as soon as the HTTP server is listening. A deep check answers "are all the dependencies this service needs reachable and responsive?" by pinging the database, the cache, the downstream services, and the message broker. Shallow checks are fast (sub-millisecond) and never produce false negatives from transient dependency blips; deep checks are slow (10–100ms) and can produce false negatives when a dependency is briefly slow. The trade-off is that shallow checks cannot detect a service that is up but functionally broken (the database connection is misconfigured, the cache is unreachable), while deep checks can but at the cost of slower probe responses and cascading false-negatives when a shared dependency blips. The best practice is a layered approach: liveness probe is shallow (process alive); readiness probe is moderately deep (process alive plus the most critical dependency — usually the database — reachable within a short timeout); a separate "deep health" endpoint exposes the full dependency tree for diagnostics but is not used for routing decisions. Teams that put deep checks on the readiness probe create a failure mode where a brief database blip removes every service instance from the load balancer simultaneously, producing a full outage from a transient condition.

The third concept is load-balancer health checks versus orchestrator health checks. A load balancer (AWS ELB, HAProxy, Envoy) probes each backend instance every N seconds and routes traffic only to healthy ones; the probe is the LB's mechanism for honoring its own health-check-driven routing. An orchestrator (Kubernetes, Nomad) probes each pod every N seconds and restarts failing pods (liveness) or removes them from the service's endpoint list (readiness); the probe is the orchestrator's mechanism for self-healing. The two operate at different layers and on different timescales — the LB probe runs every 5–10 seconds and affects routing decisions within the LB; the orchestrator probe runs every 10–30 seconds and affects pod lifecycle (restart, evict). The interaction is that the LB's health check ultimately depends on the orchestrator's: if the orchestrator removes a pod from the endpoint list, the LB (which reads the endpoint list) stops routing to it. Teams that configure only one of the two (LB probe but no orchestrator probe, or vice versa) get either no self-healing (a deadlocked process is never restarted) or no routing adjustment (a not-ready pod keeps receiving traffic until the orchestrator restarts it, which may take minutes). AWS ELB's default health check interval is 30 seconds with a healthy threshold of 2 and unhealthy threshold of 2 — meaning a failing instance is removed after ~60 seconds and reinstated after ~60 seconds, which is the right timescale for most web services but too slow for latency-sensitive systems, which tune to 5-second intervals.

The fourth concept is graceful shutdown and drain. When a service instance is being stopped (deploy, scale-down, orchestrator eviction), it should not be killed mid-request — the in-flight requests should be allowed to complete, and the load balancer should be told to stop sending new ones before the process exits. The mechanism is the SIGTERM signal: on receipt, the service stops accepting new connections, returns 503 on the health endpoint (so the LB removes it from the pool), waits for in-flight requests to drain (typically 5–30 seconds), and then exits. Kubernetes supports this with `preStop` hooks and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`; AWS ELB supports it with connection draining; Envoy supports it with drain listeners. The failure mode when this is missing is the "deploy breaks the site" pattern: the orchestrator kills pods faster than the LB's health-check interval detects the unhealthiness, so the LB keeps sending traffic to dying pods, which drop connections, which the user perceives as 502 errors. The fix is always to make the health endpoint fail fast on SIGTERM and to give the LB enough time (at least one health-check interval) to detect the failure before the process exits.

The real-world example is Kubernetes' liveness/readiness probe model, which has become the industry standard since K8s 1.0 (2015) and is now the default for any containerized deployment. AWS ELB's health check (introduced 2009 for the classic ELB) provides the same mechanism at the load-balancer layer. The combination — ELB probe at the LB layer, K8s probes at the orchestrator layer — gives two-tier self-healing: the LB adjusts routing in seconds when an instance becomes not-ready; the orchestrator restarts deadlocked instances in tens of seconds. Netflix's Hystrix (2012) and later resilience libraries added a third layer — circuit breakers that trip on consecutive failures and bypass the health check entirely — but the foundational mechanism remains the periodic probe. The trade-off in health-check design is responsiveness versus stability. A short probe interval (1 second) detects failures fast but increases probe load and produces more false negatives from transient blips; a long interval (60 seconds) is stable but takes a full minute to detect a failure. The right balance for most services is 5–10 second intervals with a healthy threshold of 2 and unhealthy threshold of 3, giving roughly 15 seconds to detect failure and 10 seconds to recover — fast enough for users to perceive a brief blip rather than an outage, slow enough to ride out transient hiccups.

### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Kubelet probe every 10s] --> B{Pod responding?}
    B -->|liveness 200| C[Pod alive, no restart]
    B -->|liveness fail x3| D[Restart pod]
    B -->|readiness 200| E[Pod in endpoint list]
    B -->|readiness fail x3| F[Remove from endpoints]
    F --> G[Service stops routing to pod]
    E --> G
    G --> H[ELB probe every 5s]
    H --> I{Backend healthy?}
    I -->|200| J[Route traffic]
    I -->|503| K[Skip backend]
    L[SIGTERM on shutdown] --> M[Return 503 immediately]
    M --> N[LB removes in ~5s]
    N --> O[Drain in-flight for 30s]
    O --> P[Exit process]
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
                 Liveness probe (shallow)
                 "is the process alive?"
+--------+       +----------+                 +-----------+
|kubelet | ----> |  pod     | 200 OK -------> | no restart|
|        |       |          | 3x fail -------> | restart   |
+--------+       +----------+                 +-----------+

                 Readiness probe (moderate depth)
                 "can this pod serve traffic now?"
+--------+       +----------+                 +-----------+
|kubelet | ----> |  pod     | 200 OK -------> | in endpoints|
|        |       |  + DB    | fail ----------> | removed    |
+--------+       +----------+                 +-----------+
                                                    |
                                                    v
                                          +--------------------+
                                          | Service endpoints  |
                                          | [p1, p2, p3, p4*]  |  * p4 removed
                                          +--------------------+
                                                    |
                                                    v
                                          +--------------------+
                                          | ELB health probe   |
                                          | every 5s, 2/2 ok   |
                                          +--------------------+
                                                    |
                                                    v
                                          +--------------------+
                                          | Route to healthy   |
                                          +--------------------+

Shutdown (SIGTERM):
  1. pod returns 503 on health endpoint immediately
  2. ELB detects in ~5s, removes from pool
  3. pod drains in-flight requests for 30s (terminationGracePeriod)
  4. pod exits cleanly (no 502 to users)
```

### Walkthrough
1. The Kubernetes kubelet probes each pod's liveness endpoint every 10 seconds with a shallow check (process alive); three consecutive failures trigger a pod restart, recovering from deadlocks.
2. The kubelet separately probes each pod's readiness endpoint with a moderately deep check (process alive plus database reachable); three consecutive failures remove the pod from the service's endpoint list, but do not restart it.
3. The service's endpoint list is consumed by the load balancer (ELB, Envoy), which also probes each backend every 5 seconds; backends returning 503 are removed from the routing pool within one probe interval.
4. On shutdown, the pod receives SIGTERM, immediately returns 503 on the health endpoint (so the LB removes it from the pool within ~5 seconds), drains in-flight requests for the grace period (30 seconds), and exits cleanly without dropping user requests.
5. The two-tier probe system gives self-healing at two timescales: the LB adjusts routing in seconds for transient failures; the orchestrator restarts deadlocked instances in tens of seconds for permanent failures.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# health_checks.py - runnable; liveness/readiness distinction with graceful shutdown
import time, threading, signal, sys
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class ServiceState:
    started_at: float
    db_connected: bool = True
    cache_connected: bool = True
    shutting_down: bool = False
    in_flight: int = 0

state = ServiceState(started_at=time.time())

class HealthHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def _send(self, code: int, body: dict):
        self.send_response(code)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(str(body).encode())

    def do_GET(self):
        # Liveness: shallow - is the process alive and serving HTTP?
        if self.path == "/healthz/live":
            if state.shutting_down:
                self._send(503, {"status": "shutting_down"})
            else:
                self._send(200, {"status": "ok", "uptime_s": round(time.time() - state.started_at, 1)})
        # Readiness: moderate depth - is the DB reachable?
        elif self.path == "/healthz/ready":
            if state.shutting_down:
                self._send(503, {"status": "shutting_down"})
            elif not state.db_connected:
                self._send(503, {"status": "not_ready", "reason": "db_disconnected"})
            else:
                self._send(200, {"status": "ready", "in_flight": state.in_flight})
        # Deep health: full dependency tree, for diagnostics only (NOT for routing)
        elif self.path == "/healthz/deep":
            self._send(200, {
                "db": "ok" if state.db_connected else "down",
                "cache": "ok" if state.cache_connected else "down",
                "in_flight": state.in_flight,
                "uptime_s": round(time.time() - state.started_at, 1),
            })
        elif self.path == "/work":
            state.in_flight += 1
            try:
                time.sleep(0.2)   # simulate request handling
                self._send(200, {"result": "done"})
            finally:
                state.in_flight -= 1
        else:
            self._send(404, {"error": "not found"})

    def log_message(self, *a): pass   # silence default logging

def simulate_db_blip():
    """Toggle DB connectivity to demonstrate readiness vs liveness."""
    time.sleep(15)
    print("[sim] DB disconnected (readiness should fail, liveness stays 200)")
    state.db_connected = False
    time.sleep(20)
    print("[sim] DB reconnected (readiness recovers)")
    state.db_connected = True

def graceful_shutdown(signum, frame):
    print("[shutdown] SIGTERM received, marking not-ready, draining...")
    state.shutting_down = True   # health returns 503 -> LB removes
    deadline = time.time() + 30  # terminationGracePeriod
    while state.in_flight > 0 and time.time() < deadline:
        time.sleep(0.5)
    print(f"[shutdown] drained, {state.in_flight} in-flight remaining, exiting")
    sys.exit(0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, graceful_shutdown)
    threading.Thread(target=simulate_db_blip, daemon=True).start()
    server = HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8080), HealthHandler)
    print("Health server on :8080  (live=/healthz/live, ready=/healthz/ready, deep=/healthz/deep)")
    server.serve_forever()
```

quiz.explanation: A liveness probe asks "is this process alive and able to make progress, or should it be restarted?" — failure triggers a restart. A readiness probe asks "is this process ready to serve traffic right now?" — failure removes the instance from the routing pool but does not restart. The two must be separate because their failure modes require different responses.
